title: Motion to Intervene and Comments of Appalachian Voices in support of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s proposed revisions to Reliability Assurance Agreement Among Load Serving Entities et al. under ER26-3515.

UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                     FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                          )                       Docket No. ER26-3515-000


                          MOTION TO INTERVENE AND COMMENTS
                               OF APPALACHIAN VOICES

        Pursuant to Rules 212 and 214 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (the

Commission) Rules of Practice and Procedure, 1 Appalachian Voices submits this motion to

intervene and comments supporting PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (PJM) proposed revisions to

its Reliability Assurance Agreement Among Load Serving Entities and the PJM Open Access

Transmission Tariff to establish Interim Resource Adequacy Service (IRAS), filed on August 13,

2026, in the above-captioned proceeding (IRAS Proposal).2

        PJM’s IRAS Proposal is an ambitious, yet narrowly tailored solution to address the

primary issue facing the region: the outsized and unprecedent development of large loads and

the unsustainable bill impacts they have created for residential ratepayers. Appalachian Voices

joined the Limited Protest of Public Interest Organizations—which supports PJM’s proposal

with four modifications—yet writes separately to highlight the IRAS Proposal’s impact on

Virginia, the birthplace of the data center boom, and address associated legal issues under the

Federal Power Act. By applying only to Load Serving Entities serving New Large Loads, whose

size and operational attributes create unique concerns for the bulk transmission system and

resource adequacy, PJM’s IRAS Proposal does not unduly discriminate. Nor does it

inappropriately cross jurisdictional lines, but will instead complement efforts already underway

to address large load integration in Virginia.


1
  18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212, 385.214 (2025).
2
  PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Proposal to Establish Interim Resource Adequacy Service and a Large Load Registry
to Address System Reliability (filed Aug. 13, 2026) (IRAS Proposal).
 I.         MOTION TO INTERVENE

           Appalachian Voices moves to intervene in this proceeding. Appalachian Voices is a non-

profit organization dedicated to bringing people together to protect the land, air, and water of

Central and Southern Appalachia and advance a just transition to an equitable clean energy

economy. Appalachian Voices strives to shift to clean, 21 st-century energy sources, including

energy efficiency and low-emitting power sources, and stand up to monopoly utility practices

that put profits over people. Its ultimate goal is to establish economic solutions that create

community wealth and sustain Appalachia’s mountains, forests, and waters.

           Appalachian Voices has a substantial number of dues-paying members living in the PJM

footprint, primarily in Virginia and North Carolina. The outcome of this proceeding will impact

the reliability of PJM’s system during constrained periods, the procurement of generation to

supply large loads, and capacity costs that feed into retail rates. Accordingly, Appalachian

Voices has a substantial interest in this proceeding that cannot be adequately represented by any

other party. Further, by virtue of its organizational mission, Appalachian Voices’ participation in

this proceeding is in the public interest. Pursuant to Rule 214 of the Commission’s Rules of

Practice and Procedure,3 Appalachian Voices respectfully requests that the Commission grant it

full rights associated with party status in this proceeding.

II.        COMMENTS

           A. The Commission Should Accept PJM’s IRAS Proposal to Help Ensure that New
              Large Loads Pay their Fair Share of Capacity Costs and Bear Appropriate
              Reliability Burdens.

                   1. The IRAS Proposal Can Enable More Equitable Cost Allocation for Virginia
                      Ratepayers.




3
    18 C.F.R. § 385.214.

                                                  2
         Virginia originated the data center boom and remains its epicenter. As of late 2024, it

was home to thirteen percent of global data center capacity and twenty-five percent of data

center capacity in the Americas.4 This trend only projects to accelerate.5 The heavy

concentration of data center load in the state places significant demand on its electric grid.

Dominion Energy Virginia (Dominion), a vertically integrated utility and PJM Transmission

Owner, has asserted that “no other utility in the country has the magnitude of high load demand

that Virginia is facing.”6 The utility has argued that the “scale, density of data center

development, and load that [Dominion] must support significantly outpace[s]” other markets,

making it a “uniquely concentrated and capital-intensive environment.” 7 State and federal

policies are only just now starting to catch up to the drastic changes that data centers have

imposed on the state’s electric power system.

        Traditional approaches to wholesale and retail cost allocation have had the effect of

socializing the cost of procuring capacity for large loads across the broader customer base. As a

vertically integrated utility subject to state integrated resource planning requirements, Dominion

owns or contracts for the majority of the generating capacity needed to meet its native load

requirements, including New Large Load customers. 8 It procures the remaining increment that it

 cannot self-supply from PJM’s Base Residual Auction (BRA). 9 While this arrangement may act

as a hedge against BRA clearing prices for most of Dominion’s capacity requirements,

Dominion’s retail customers still must cover the capital costs of Dominion’s generation holdings

through base retail rates. And as Dominion pursues significant buildout of new generating

capacity to meet its burgeoning large load growth,10 residential customers will necessarily bear

the cost burden of those new facilities. Further, as described below, BRA clearing prices have

skyrocketed in recent years due to large load growth, particularly in the DOM zone that covers

Dominion’s territory.11 When Dominion does not have sufficient self-supply capacity to serve

its native load, that load must pay the BRA prices associated with covering the shortfall. 12

        The IRAS Proposal could help to alleviate these cost burdens on Virginia ratepayers in at

least three ways.

        First, by requiring Load Serving Entities to “bring new capacity in an amount that equals

or exceeds its New Large Loads’ peak load or be subject to load reduction requests,” 13 the IRAS

Proposal dictates that Dominion procure capacity dedicated to serving discrete New Large

Loads. Absent explicit matching of this new capacity with one or more New Large Loads,

Dominion’s load will face curtailment exposure. This connect-the-dots requirement will enable

the Virginia State Corporation Commission (SCC) to identify generation capacity costs caused

by New Large Loads and allocate those costs accordingly. In other words, the IRAS Proposal

should prevent Dominion from continuing to commingle capacity costs caused by New Large

        Second, the IRAS Proposal creates a Large Load Registry that will provide the SCC and

other regulatory entities greater visibility into the New Large Loads seeking service in a given

Electric Distributor footprint.14 The Large Load Registry will identify, among other things, the

specific Bring Your Own New Capacity associated with the New Large Load. 15 This will

similarly provide the transparency needed to appropriately allocate capacity costs in retail rates

and effectuate the Ratepayer Protection Pledge signed by Dominion and most data center

developers.16 It also mirrors the obligation and intended effect of the Commission’s Show Cause

directive that PJM identify network upgrade costs caused by large loads so that state regulators

may account for that information when allocating costs at the retail level. 17

        Third, by excluding New Large Load that does not bring its own capacity from the

Variable Resource Requirement curve in future Reliability Pricing Model (RPM) auctions, 18 the

IRAS Proposal will protect Virginia residential customers from excessive PJM-derived capacity

costs going forward. This will impact both (1) Dominion customers who must cover the RPM

costs for the increment of capacity obligations that Dominion does not self-supply, and

(2) customers of the state’s electric cooperatives, which rely more heavily on RPM auctions for

their capacity needs.

          Together, these aspects of the IRAS Proposal better enable the SCC and the state’s

cooperative utilities to quarantine capacity costs needed to serve New Large Load growth from

the bills of residential retail customers.

                  2. PJM’s Solution Is Narrowly Tailored to Maintain Reliability and Ensure that
                     New Large Loads Pay their Fair Share of Capacity Costs.

         Without appropriate protective measures, large loads will continue to jeopardize

reliability and affordability in the PJM region. PJM’s RPM, the mechanism created to enable the

delivery of reliable capacity to PJM’s system, has failed to procure enough capacity to meet

PJM’s reliability requirement two years in a row. The BRA for the 2027/2028 Delivery Year

cleared 6,623 MW short of the PJM Region Reliability Requirement and at the price cap of

$333.44/MW-day.19 The BRA for the 2028/2029 Delivery Year, held this summer, cleared

6,831.3 MW short and also hit the market price cap of $325/MW-day. 20 Large load development

is the principal cause for PJM’s market clearing short and reaching the price cap. 21

         Subjecting Load Serving Entities that serve New Large Loads and have not arranged for

their required capacity to IRAS appropriately balances two competing concerns. On one hand,

the IRAS Proposal appropriately protects regular ratepayers from reliability and cost impacts

caused by New Large Loads. As the primary drivers of the capacity shortfall, large loads and the

Load Serving Entities that procure capacity on their behalf should be responsible for securing

and paying for sufficient capacity to meet their demand. To the extent New Large Loads and/or

their Load Serving Entities are unable to bring sufficient capacity online in time to meet their

demand, it is just and reasonable to keep those New Large Loads out of the capacity market and

21

2026) (“The current conditions are not the result of organic load growth. The current conditions in the capacity

                                                          6
 subject their Load Serving Entity to IRAS. Doing so will insulate regular customers from load

shed events that would not likely to occur but for the addition of power-hungry New Large

Loads. On the other hand, New Large Loads seek speed to power. PJM’s IRAS Proposal offers

a viable path for New Large Loads to come online faster than the generation needed to meet their

demand and will only subject those New Large Loads to load reduction requests during

Emergencies prior to Pre-Emergency Load Management Response. 22 This properly places the

responsibility for resolving challenges related to the capacity market shortfalls with New Large

Loads and their Load Serving Entities without imposing undue burden on those entities.

         B. The IRAS Proposal Reflects an Appropriate Exercise of Jurisdiction under the
            Federal Power Act and Will Complement Virginia’s Efforts to Integrate Large
            Loads.

         PJM’s proposal also respects jurisdictional boundaries and initiatives underway in the

states seeking to address the challenges that large load integration presents. The Federal Power

Act grants the Commission jurisdiction over “the transmission of electric energy in interstate

commerce and the sale of electric energy at wholesale in interstate commerce[.]” 23 The states

maintain jurisdiction over “facilities used for the generation of electric energy or over facilities

used in local distribution[.]”24 The Federal Power Act also reserves for the states jurisdiction

over retail sales, i.e., sales to end-use customers. 25

         The IRAS Proposal represents a proper exercise of the Commission’s authority over the

interstate transmission system. Order No. 2000 establishes Regional Transmission

Organizations’ (RTO) authority over transmission operations, which obligates RTOs like PJM to

 operate as security coordinator for the region. 26 PJM’s role as security coordinator requires it to

monitor real-time system conditions and to “direct[] actions to maintain reliability, including

firm load shedding.”27 PJM’s proposal to direct Electric Distributors to shed load falls squarely

within PJM’s authority to operate the transmission system and coordinate relief procedures.

        Nor does PJM’s IRAS Proposal tread on state authority over retail sales. Although PJM

proposes to issue load reduction directives to Electric Distributors, PJM defers to the Electric

Distributors and the relevant states to resolve how to prioritize load reductions in their service

territories.28 PJM’s IRAS Proposal neither mandates nor prohibits load shed of specific end-use

customers, but rather mandates that Electric Distributors shed an aggregate number of megawatts

that matches the capacity of Eligible New Large Loads.29 That Electric Distributors should

direct curtailment of New Large Loads is an expectation, not a PJM requirement. Ultimately, the

Electric Distributor, working in conjunction with the relevant state regulator, must develop and

execute the appropriate retail load curtailment protocols. Tying the megawatt quantity to be shed

to New Large Loads is matter of reliability and cost causation. New Large Loads have caused

the capacity shortfall in PJM; it would be unjust and unreasonable to shed residential load due to

insufficient capacity to meet New Large Load demand.

        The Commission also has authority over generation facilities to the extent those facilities

are needed to ensure transmission system reliability.30 As an operator of the bulk-power system,

which includes “electric energy from generation facilities needed to maintain transmission

system reliability[,]”31 PJM has an obligation to comply with reliability standards set pursuant to

 section 215 of the Federal Power Act. Combined with PJM’s authority as security coordinator

for the region, the responsibility to maintain system reliability enables PJM to condition

transmission service during times of system stress on either the New Large Load or the Load

Serving Entity that serves it securing sufficient capacity to meet the large load’s demand. If PJM

were to require that the New Large Load or Load Serving Entity select a certain resource type to

cover the New Large Load’s demand, that would intrude on state authority, but that is not what

PJM has proposed.

         Indeed, PJM’s IRAS Proposal enables effective cooperative federalism by

complementing efforts in Virginia to ensure orderly integration of large loads. The SCC has

approved tariff changes proposed by Dominion and Appalachian Power Company to address

large loads, both of which define large loads and require collateral, minimum contract terms, and

minimum demand charges.32 These tariff changes operate within the state’s jurisdiction over

retail sales and aim to ensure that large loads pay for stranded costs associated with generation,

transmission, and distribution costs should the large load not materialize. PJM’s IRAS Proposal,

by contrast, operates within the Commission’s jurisdiction over transmission service and bulk

power system reliability33 to provide for interim service to the extent that New Large Loads and

their Load Serving Entities in Virginia cannot secure sufficient capacity to meet their need by the

desired in-service date. It does so without jeopardizing transmission system reliability or

saddling regular ratepayers with the costs of securing capacity to integrate New Large Loads.

         C. The IRAS Proposal Does Not Unduly Discriminate.

        PJM’s IRAS Proposal is not unduly discriminatory because any such differentiation

among capacity buyers is warranted by the size, operational characteristics, and grid impacts

caused by New Large Load. The United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia

Circuit (D.C. Circuit) has held that discrimination is undue only if differently treated entities are

“similarly situated,”34 such that “there is no reason for the difference.” 35 There is no undue

discrimination where the Commission articulates relevant, significant facts to provide a rational

basis for treating two entities differently, 36 and the Commission has “wide discretion . . . to

determine what constitute[s]” undue discrimination. 37

        The D.C. Circuit has specifically held that utilities may discriminate between two entities

due to capacity constraints. In Complex Consolidated Edison Company v. FERC, the

Commission upheld differential treatment of two natural gas pipeline customers on this basis.

The Commission found in the underlying order that, without the pipeline company’s disparate

treatment of two different customers, one customer “could pull enough gas off the system to

leave inadequate quantities available to meet other customers’” needs. 38 The D.C. Circuit

affirmed the Commission’s decision, stating that “the Commission gave an adequate explanation

of how it reached its conclusion that there was no undue discrimination[.]” 39 Further, the court

found that “a rational, non-discriminatory basis existed for the difference in situation, namely

operational constraints.”40

         A similar principle underlies the treatment at issue here. PJM expects to experience 29.7

gigawatts of load growth between 2025 and 2030. 41 According to the Independent Market

Monitor for PJM, “[d]ata center load growth is the primary reason for recent and expected

capacity market conditions, including total forecast load growth, the tight supply and demand

balance, and high prices[.]”42 Accordingly, it is reasonable to assume that any requirement to

meet 100 percent of data center demand 100 percent of the time would jeopardize PJM’s ability

to meet the demand of existing residential customers, given the current capacity constraints. For

this reason, a policy that requires only Load Serving Entities serving New Large Loads to match

this demand with sufficient capacity or for the New Large Loads themselves to bring their own

new capacity or be subject to IRAS, is not undue discrimination. Here, the distinction between

New Large Loads and existing load is based on legitimate operational constraints in PJM created

by a sudden and unprecedented influx of large load demand. Managing these operational

constraints therefore provides a rational basis for differential treatment between Load Serving

Entities serving New Large Loads relative to all other load.

        The D.C. Circuit has also found that public utilities may discriminate between two

entities based on different customer characteristics. In Cities of Bethany, et al. v. FERC, the

D.C. Circuit upheld the Commission’s approval of separate customer categories where two

entities “have different customer profiles and load characteristics[.]” 43 PJM’s IRAS Proposal

likewise applies differential treatment to Load Serving Entities serving New Large Loads

compared to all other load based on different customer profiles and load characteristics. As

 compared to existing residential and commercial customers, large loads have significantly higher

demand requirements. PJM’s IRAS Proposal classifies New Large Loads as those requiring 50

MW or more,44 but large loads can require several hundred or even a thousand megawatts. 45

Moreover, many large loads have high load factors that far exceed the average load factor of

residential customers. As such, large loads both demand significant amounts of power and run

constantly, which differs markedly from traditional load profiles. As the Commission has

acknowledged, “integrating large loads poses specific challenges to transmission system

operation given their size, operational behavior, and unique potential to impact the transmission

system.”46 Therefore, categorizing and treating Load Serving Entities that serve New Large

Loads separately from existing load is not unduly discriminatory.

        In fact, imposing a single rate regime covering service to both traditional load and New

Large Loads may itself be unduly discriminatory. In Alabama Electric Co-op., Inc. v. FERC, the

D.C. Circuit held that a single rate design that places on one group of customers “charges which

are higher than necessary to recover the costs of servicing that group” may be unlawfully

discriminatory.47 The court explained that a reasonable rate scheme “should produce revenues

from each class of customers which match, as closely as practicable, the cost to serve each class

or individual customer.”48 The rapid influx of large load demand is the principal driver of the

generation capacity shortfall and price spikes in the PJM region, 49 causing residential and

commercial customers to pay more than the costs required to service their own needs. To

ameliorate this unduly discriminatory rate regime, PJM has appropriately proposed differential

III.   CONCLUSION

       For the foregoing reasons, Appalachian Voices respectfully requests that the Commission

approve PJM’s IRAS Proposal.
